questions.q: Per this lesson, what's the key difference between the Lesson 13 dashboard and an executive update?
options: The dashboard is built for exploring; the executive update is a fixed, short artifact that answers "fund this or not" without requiring any clicking
They are the same thing with different color schemes
The executive update must contain more raw data than the dashboard
The dashboard is only for executives and the update is only for stewards
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts an explorable dashboard with a fixed artifact meant to be read without clicking.

questions.q: What is the first element of the four-part executive update structure this lesson describes?
options: A one-line verdict — on track, at risk, or behind — stated plainly
A detailed appendix of every KPI
A list of everyone on the governance team
A history of the program since it launched
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the verdict comes first, not buried after several paragraphs of context.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what happens when a program's reporting consistently softens bad news into something more palatable?
options: Trust erodes — once an executive catches one overly optimistic update, future "on track" reports get read with suspicion
Nothing changes; executives never notice
The program automatically gets more funding
It has no effect on how future updates are received
questions.explain: The lesson warns that softened bad news backfires: it damages the credibility of every future update, including honest ones.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend doing immediately after stating an honest "at risk" or "behind" verdict?
options: Pairing it with the specific reason why, such as a staffing gap or a slipped dependency
Changing the verdict to something more positive
Ending the update immediately with no further explanation
Waiting until the next quarter to explain why
questions.explain: The lesson's guidance is to pair the honest verdict immediately with a specific reason, rather than letting the number speak for itself.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say reporting cadence matters as much as the report's content?
options: An irregular update schedule trains the audience to stop expecting updates, making the program easy to deprioritize or cut
Cadence has no real effect on how a program is perceived
More frequent reporting is always better regardless of content
Cadence only matters for board-level reporting, not steering committees
questions.explain: The lesson argues a predictable cadence keeps governance visible as a standing item, while irregular reporting makes it easy to forget or cut.
